docs.title: OpenDNA
docs.text:
Protein property prediction that runs on your own machine. No server, no account, no network: sequences stay where you opened them.

Four trained models score candidate sequences for per-residue disorder, per-residue solvent accessibility, solubility, and the stability effect of a point mutation, from a command line or a desktop application. The disorder head is competitive with the CAID3 field — AUROC 0.941 on Disorder-PDB, against published figures of 0.925 for AIUPred v3 and 0.954 for MUSE-IDR.

The reason to use it is usually not that it predicts better, but that it predicts at all somewhere that sending unpublished sequences to a vendor is not allowed.

If you have to sign off on using this for real work, start with Validation: what has been checked, how, and what has not.

This documentation set is deliberately thin. OpenDNA was rewritten from a Python service with a React front end into Rust, and most of what used to be here described the Python REST API, its deployment and its analysis engines — all of which have been removed. Pages that documented them have been deleted rather than left to describe software that no longer exists.

The changelog lists what the rewrite removed, and the roadmap what is unfinished.

The accurate documentation lives next to the code it describes:

Project overview and model accuracy what works, what does not, and how the heads score on external benchmarks Development guide workspace layout, builds, GPU setup, the ground rules Datasets sources, licences, construction, reproducibility Training embedding caches, training the heads, external benchmarks Models the trained heads, their cards, and publishing Command line batch predictions over a FASTA file CAID submissions the assessment format, and the two ways it fails silently Pipelines running parts in parallel under Nextflow or Snakemake

Each trained head carries its own model card stating its baseline, its measured metrics, and its limitations.

docs.title: What it does not do
docs.text: Earlier documentation advertised structure prediction, docking, molecular dynamics, sequence design, antibody modelling, and an HTTP API. None of those exists, and none is planned — see the roadmap. They are listed here because a reader who remembers the old pages deserves a straight answer rather than silence.

docs.title: Changelog
docs.text:
Entries are written for somebody deciding whether to upgrade, so removals come first and known limitations are stated rather than left to be discovered.

Versions follow semantic versioning. The project is pre-1.0: the command-line interface, the file formats and the head metadata schema may still change between minor versions, and when they do it will be said here.

docs.title: v0.6.0-rc1 — unreleased
docs.text:
A rewrite, not an upgrade. Everything between v0.5.0-rc1 and here replaced the Python backend and the React front end with Rust. Most of what v0.5.x advertised no longer exists. Read the removals before upgrading.

A release candidate rather than a release because of what has not been exercised: this tag is the first thing the release workflow has ever built, the macOS and Linux installers have never been produced on any machine, and the installers are unsigned. The command-line tool is the part that has been measured and tested.

The desktop application reports version 0.6.0 rather than 0.6.0-rc1. The MSI bundler requires a pre-release identifier to be numeric, so rc1 would fail the Windows build outright; the JSON it is configured in cannot carry a comment saying so, which is why it is said here.

docs.title: Removed
docs.text:
• The Python backend and the React user interface. Both are gone from the repository, along with the FastAPI server, the PyInstaller sidecar and the wheel.
  • ESMFold structure prediction. No structures are predicted. The desktop application can open and view a PDB or mmCIF file you already have.
  • ESM-IF1 inverse folding. No sequence design.
  • Molecular dynamics. No simulation of any kind.
  • The antibody and plasmid tools, the model hub and the project templates. These were added after v0.5.0-rc1 and were never part of a tagged release: a commit calls itself v0.5.0-rc2 but no such tag exists.
  • The deployment configuration for running OpenDNA as a server. It is not a server; it opens no network port.

If you depend on any of these, stay on v0.5.0-rc1, the last release that has them. They are not coming back in this line: the reason for the rewrite was that a platform advertising nine things it did badly was worth less than a tool doing four things with numbers attached.

docs.title: Added — four trained heads with measured accuracy
docs.text:
Each predicts one property from frozen ESM-2 150M embeddings, and each ships a model card generated from its own training report.

Head In-domain test External Disorder AUROC 0.883 AUROC 0.941 on CAID3 Disorder-PDB Accessibility (burial) Spearman 0.737 not benchmarked externally Stability (ΔΔG) Spearman 0.674 Spearman 0.442 over 4 ProteinGym assays Solubility Spearman 0.701 none exists under usable terms

Disorder is the strong one and sits inside the published CAID3 field. Stability is a ranking signal and the in-domain figure overstates generalisation by about 0.23 Spearman — the README says so beside the table, and so does the card. ESM-2 650M was tried and rejected: it made disorder worse on every external metric for four times the weights.

A missing head is an error naming the files it looked for. Nothing falls back to a heuristic and reports it as a prediction.

docs.title: Added — a command-line tool
docs.text:
opendna runs the heads over a FASTA file and writes a table. The desktop application works on one protein at a time, which is the wrong shape for triaging a few hundred candidates.

  • predict for all four tasks, in csv, tsv, json or caid format.
  • models lists what is installed, verifies each head's weights against the digest in its metadata, and can write or check a lockfile.
  • selftest runs the installed heads over a bundled sequence and checks 18 recorded values and invariants. It exists because models passes a correct install with the wrong weights in it — the files are intact and the numbers are wrong, and only running them catches that.
  • stage copies an installation, embedding model included, into one directory that works on a machine with no network.
  • split and merge for running parts in parallel. merge reads each part's manifest and refuses to join parts produced by different software, on different devices or at different batch sizes, which cat cannot notice.
  • --checkpoint records results as they are produced and continues an interrupted run from the last complete chunk. Verified byte-identical to an uninterrupted run, including after a real process kill.

docs.title: Added — provenance, so a number can be defended
docs.text:
• Every head has a build id, derived from its weights, its training configuration and its data, that a lab can pin and verify.
  • Every output file carries the head version, the embedding model, the device and the card's limitations as comments, taken from the card rather than written twice.
  • Every run writes a manifest beside its output: the input's digest, the output's digest, the head build, the weights digest, the device, the batch size, the chunk size, the licence and how long it took.
  • Licences travel with the weights. One head is trained on share-alike data and released on the same terms; stage writes a LICENSES.md grouping the heads by licence and flagging that one, because a result passed on without it is an obligation somebody does not know they have.
  • The exit status says what to do about the failure: 2 for usage, 3 for the installation, 4 for the input, 5 for a failed check, 1 for anything unanticipated. Checked against the compiled binary.

docs.title: Added — what the numbers mean, measured rather than asserted
docs.text:
• Disorder probabilities are calibrated. They were inflated about threefold by class-weighted training; where the head said 0.55, 13% of residues were disordered. Platt scaling on held-out data fixed the scale and moved the decision threshold, which the head now records and the CLI and the application both read, so the two cannot disagree. Calibration changed the meaning of the number and not the ranking: AUROC is identical before and after.
  • Confidence predicts error, and abstaining helps. The distance from the threshold recovers 55% of the reduction in error that a perfect oracle would give. --min-confidence marks rows below a cut-off against the head's own measured trade-off, and never removes them: a table quietly missing rows looks exactly like a complete one. A k-mer novelty signal was tested, found worse than random, and the rejection is recorded so nobody re-tests it.
  • The regressors report prediction intervals. Split conformal on the validation split: ±1.33 kcal/mol for stability at 90% (achieving 93.7%), ±38.9 percentage points for solubility, ±0.237 RSA for burial. Coverage achieved is printed beside the level asked for because they differ — burial undercovers at every level, since clustering the splits by sequence identity breaks the exchangeability conformal assumes.

docs.title: Added — the supporting workspaces
docs.text:
• datasets/ builds all four datasets from primary sources, clusters by sequence identity so near-identical proteins cannot straddle a split, and commits a card recording exactly what it produced.
  • training/ trains, benchmarks, calibrates, measures abstention and fits intervals, and generates each head's card from the measured report.
  • pipelines/ holds Nextflow and Snakemake modules. Neither has been run against its engine; what has been verified is the behaviour they rely on.
  • docs/VALIDATION.md is written for whoever has to sign this off, and includes a section on what has not been checked.

docs.title: Changed
docs.text:
• The desktop application is Tauri 2 with a Leptos front end compiled to WebAssembly. No Node toolchain, no bundled Python.
  • CI builds and tests on Windows, macOS and Linux, audits dependencies, and checks the minimum supported Rust version (1.95).
  • The dependency audit passes again. cargo deny check licenses had been failing, so the CI audit job was red: three dependencies carry licences the allow list did not cover. Two of them, colored and option-ext, are MPL-2.0 and reach the shipped binary through the Hugging Face client, and hf-hub 1.0 has no feature that drops it. They are now allowed with the reason recorded in deny.toml and disclosed in the command-line README and the release notes, rather than by widening the list quietly.
  • The Dockerfile builds the command-line tool. The previous one built a Python API server from directories the rewrite deleted, so it could not have worked. The new one is multi-stage, runs as a non-root user, exposes no port, and is built and smoke-tested by CI on every commit because the machine it was written on has Docker installed but not running.
  • MODEL_CARD.md and docs/ROADMAP.md were rewritten. Both described the removed software: the first carried cards for ESMFold, ESM-IF1 and ProteinMPNN, and the second listed nineteen phases of it as done. CITATION.cff likewise still claimed version 0.4.0 and an abstract about structure prediction and inverse folding.
  • unsafe code is forbidden in the three workspaces that ship: the root crates, the desktop application and the training tools. The dataset builder is a maintainers' tool and is not covered.

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
• No signed installers. Operating systems will warn. Code-signing certificates have not been obtained.
  • Two runs cannot load the embedding model through the Hugging Face cache at once; on Windows the second is refused the weights file. Run opendna stage once and point --models at the bundle, which several runs can share. This matters because split and the pipelines exist to run parts side by side.
  • One machine. Every measurement in the documentation comes from a single Windows workstation with an RTX 2000 Ada. Cross-platform numerical agreement is untested.
  • No clinical or diagnostic validation of any kind.
  • Nothing detects out-of-domain input. The disorder head's confidence predicts error, which is not the same thing.

docs.title: Fixed (the actual root cause of all desktop app auto-start issues)
docs.text:
• Pipe deadlock in Tauri sidecar: previous code spawned the Python API server with Stdio::piped() for stdout/stderr but never read from those pipes. uvicorn's startup output filled the pipe buffer within seconds and the child process froze on write() before opening port 8765. Fix: use Stdio::null() so the child can never block on parent I/O.
  • Console window popup on Windows: every Python sidecar spawn produced a black cmd.exe window. Fix: added CREATE_NO_WINDOW = 0x08000000 flag (Windows-specific) via the new configure_child_command() helper. Applied to all child process spawns.
  • VERIFIED LOCALLY with npx tauri build: built opendna-desktop.exe, killed all running Python processes, launched the desktop app, watched logs say Sidecar startup: Started API server, and confirmed curl http://127.0.0.1:8765/health returned 200 OK with no manual intervention.

docs.title: Roadmap
docs.text:
What is coming next, and what is not.

This file was rewritten for v0.6.0-rc1. The version before it listed nineteen phases of a Python application as done — structure prediction, docking, molecular dynamics, a plugin marketplace, a VR mode — none of which exists any more. Leaving it in place would have made the published roadmap contradict the software it was shipped with.

docs.title: Current status: v0.6.0-rc1
docs.text:
Four trained heads over frozen ESM-2 embeddings — disorder, solvent accessibility, stability and solubility — with a command-line tool for batch work and a Tauri desktop application with a structure viewer. Everything a prediction rests on is recorded: head build, weights digest, device, batch and chunk size, input and output digests, and the limitations from the model card.

The command-line tool is the measured and tested part. What makes this a release candidate rather than a release is below.

docs.title: Before dropping the -rc1
docs.text:
In order. Each is a thing that is currently unknown or unfinished, not a feature.

  • Produce the artefacts at all. The release workflow has never run. The tag that triggers it is its first test, and no installer has ever been built on macOS or Linux.
  • Signed installers. Apple notarization, Windows Authenticode, GPG for the AppImage. Blocked on obtaining certificates, which costs money rather than effort.
  • Agree across platforms. Every number in the documentation comes from one Windows workstation. CI builds and tests on three operating systems, but nothing has checked that they produce the same values. opendna selftest is the tool for this; it needs running on the other two.
  • Load the embedding model concurrently. Two runs cannot read the Hugging Face cache at the same time; on Windows the second is refused the weights file. Staging a bundle works around it and is documented, but a tool whose own split command exists to run parts in parallel should not need a workaround for it.
  • Let selftest check the heads that are present. It needs all four installed and exits 3 with fewer, which is wrong for the common case: a lab that wants only disorder cannot verify the head it has. opendna models hashes the weights against their recorded digest and works on one head, so the model cards point there instead, but the stronger check should not be all-or-nothing.
  • Check resuming at the scale it is for. --checkpoint is verified byte-identical across an interruption on runs of a few chunks, including a real process kill. Nothing has tested a run of tens of thousands of sequences interrupted hours in, and none of it has been repeated on a GPU.

docs.title: After that
docs.text: Ordered by how much it would change what somebody can conclude from a result.

docs.title: Measurement
docs.text:
• An external benchmark for solubility and accessibility. Neither has one. For solubility the obstacle is real: the reference sets are behind terms that forbid redistribution or belong to retired services. Saying there is no number beats quoting the in-domain figure as though it were comparable, but it is still a gap.
  • A CAID entry rather than a reimplementation. The 0.941 on CAID3 Disorder-PDB was produced by running the published protocol against the reference file, independently recomputed in numpy, and is not an official entry. The CAID4 deadline needs checking.
  • Out-of-domain detection. The disorder head's confidence predicts error, which is not the same thing: a sequence from a family it never saw can still produce a confident wrong answer. The one proxy tried here — whether a residue's 5-mer appeared in training — carried no information at all, and that rejection is recorded so it is not retried blindly.
  • Intervals that vary with the input. Split conformal gives a constant half-width, so a regressor's interval is wider than it needs to be where the head is reliable and narrower where it is not. The conditional coverage on each card shows where. A normalised or locally adaptive variant would fix the shape; it also needs more held-out data than some of these splits have.
  • Honest coverage for accessibility. Its intervals undercover at every level, because clustering the splits by sequence identity breaks the exchangeability conformal assumes. Clustering is the right way to build the splits, so the fix is a method that does not need the assumption.

docs.title: Operations
docs.text:
• Run the pipelines against their engines. The Nextflow and Snakemake modules have never been executed by Nextflow or Snakemake: neither is installed on the machine they were written on. What is verified is the behaviour they depend on.
  • Resume inside a pipeline. Both engines give a retried task a fresh working directory, so a checkpoint has to live somewhere that outlives the attempt. Where that is depends on the cluster's filesystem.
  • A GPU other than one. The finding that batching costs time on a GPU comes from a single RTX 2000 Ada. --batch-tokens exists so somebody can measure theirs.

docs.title: Possibly
docs.text:
Not promised, and each would need its own justification before being started.

  • More heads, where a dataset exists that can be redistributed and a baseline exists to be measured against.
  • A larger embedding model, if one ever helps. ESM-2 650M was tried and rejected: it made disorder worse on every external metric for four times the weights.
  • Structure-aware features, now that the accessibility head exists.

docs.title: Not planned
docs.text:
Stated so nobody waits for them. All of these were advertised by v0.5.x and removed in the rewrite:

  • Structure prediction, inverse folding, docking, molecular dynamics, free energy perturbation
  • Antibody-specific models, plasmid tools, a model hub, project templates
  • A server deployment, a plugin marketplace, real-time co-editing, a VR mode

The reason for removing them is the reason for not planning them: a platform advertising nine things it did badly was worth less than a tool doing four things with numbers attached. Anything added back has to arrive with a measured number and a stated baseline, like the four heads did.

docs.title: Versioning
docs.text:
Semantic versioning: MAJOR.MINOR.PATCH[-pre].

Pre-1.0, the command-line interface, the output formats and the head metadata schema may change between minor versions. When they do, the changelog says so. Head versions are separate from the project's: a head carries its own version and a build id derived from its weights, configuration and data, so a result can be traced to the exact model that produced it regardless of which release ran it.

docs.title: Contributing to the roadmap
docs.text: Open an issue or a pull request with the use case, a rough idea of the effort, and what it depends on. For anything in the Measurement section, the most useful contribution is a number: a benchmark run, a reference set that can be redistributed, or a counter-measurement on hardware that is not this one.

docs.title: Validation
docs.text:
This page is for whoever has to sign off on using OpenDNA for real work: a QA reviewer, a core facility lead, somebody writing a methods section. It states what has been checked, by whom, how, and what has not been.

It is not a claim that OpenDNA is validated for your purpose. Validation is against an intended use, and only you know yours. What this gives you is the evidence to do that assessment, and an honest account of where the evidence runs out.

Everything below was measured on the hardware named with it. Where a number comes from one machine, it says so, because a number from one machine is weaker evidence than it looks.

docs.title: What the software is
docs.text:
Four small networks on top of frozen ESM-2 embeddings. The language model is never fine-tuned, so each head is a few hundred kilobytes of weights over a 568 MB embedding model that is itself a published third-party checkpoint (facebook/esm2_t30_150M_UR50D).

Head Predicts Honest out-of-domain performance disorder per-residue intrinsic disorder AUROC 0.941 on CAID3 Disorder-PDB burial per-residue relative solvent accessibility see model card solubility whole-protein solubility, E. coli cell-free see model card stability ΔΔG for a named point substitution ~0.44 Spearman out of domain

The stability figure is the one to read carefully. 0.44 Spearman makes it a ranking signal for prioritising constructs, not a measurement of ΔΔG. Each head's model card states its own limitations and the CLI copies them into every output file, so a number cannot travel without them.

There is no fallback anywhere. A missing head is an error naming the files it looked for. A sequence too long for the solubility head is refused rather than scored by a different method. Nothing in OpenDNA estimates a property without a trained model for it.

docs.title: Can I identify what I ran?
docs.text:
Yes, and it is checkable rather than asserted.

Each head records a semantic version, a build id digesting everything that determined the weights (the dataset manifest, the hyperparameters, the embedding model, the training code version), and the SHA-256 of its weights file. opendna models rehashes the weights and reports verified, NOT VERIFIABLE (metadata predating hashes) or CORRUPT.

opendna models --lock models.lock    # pin
opendna models --check models.lock   # fail unless the install is still that

--check catches a retrain that kept the same version number, because the build id changes even when the version does not. Commit the lockfile beside the analysis it produced.

Checked: appending one byte to a weights file is reported CORRUPT, makes opendna models exit 3, and makes opendna predict refuse before loading anything. A head whose build id differs from a lockfile fails --check with both values named.

docs.title: Can I prove it works on this machine?
docs.text:
opendna selftest

Seventeen checks over a bundled ubiquitin sequence, through the same code path predict uses rather than a parallel harness. Eight are invariants that hold for any build of these heads — one value per residue, probabilities within [0,1], accessibility within [0,1.25], the hydrophobic core less accessible than the chain-forming lysines, L8P more destabilising than L8M, and a second identical run giving identical values. Nine are numbers recorded from named builds, with tolerances.

A pinned number is checked only against the build it was recorded from. Against another build it reports not checked and names both, because nobody has measured what that head does on this fixture. A retrain is therefore expected to leave those unchecked until new values are recorded; the invariants still run.

Checked, and this is the part worth reading: burial's weights were copied over the disorder head and the metadata rewritten so the file hashes correctly. opendna models passed that installation completely clean — every head verified. The self-test failed three pinned checks and exited 5. A checksum cannot detect a model that is intact and wrong; this can.

The fixture's positions were chosen for that case. Disorder and burial share an architecture and differ only in the squash on the output, so at some positions their numbers agree to 0.004 and a pin there would survive the swap. The positions used are ones where the two disagree by more than a quarter.

Tolerances are a judgement, not a measurement. They were set wide enough to absorb a different BLAS or device and narrow enough that a wrong model fails. A failure that lands just outside one is worth reporting, not widening.

docs.title: How reproducible are the numbers?
docs.text:
Exactly this much:

Same input, same device, same --batch-tokens byte-identical Same input, same device, different --batch-tokens ~0.2% of values differ Same input, CPU vs GPU ~0.3% of values differ

Measured on 200 sequences and 35,033 residues. Across devices, 102 of 35,033 disorder probabilities differed, by at most 0.0001 and 0.0000003 on average. That is the f32 rounding floor, not a disagreement about biology, and it moves no disorder call at any sensible threshold.

It does mean a result file from a GPU and one from a CPU are not the same bytes. Do not diff them and do not compare their checksums.

The cause in both cases is the order of floating-point summation: padding changes it, and so does different silicon. Device and batch size are recorded in every run manifest, which makes the table above checkable — two manifests agreeing on input digest, head build, device and batch size should have produced the same output digest, and if they did not, something is wrong worth finding.

Driving one model from several threads at once on CUDA perturbs the low bits, because cuBLAS picks differently shaped reductions under concurrent load. The CLI is serial, which is why.

Checked: byte-identical repeat runs on both CPU and an RTX 2000 Ada. All seventeen self-test checks pass on both, with values pinned on CPU.

docs.title: Do the probabilities mean anything?
docs.text:
For the disorder head, now yes, and the correction was substantial.

The head is trained with weighted cross-entropy so that it does not predict "ordered" everywhere. That helps the ranking and inflates the probabilities, and the inflation was never measured. It is large:

the head said actually disordered 0.95 65% 0.85 50% 0.75 32% 0.55 13%

Expected calibration error on the held-out split was 0.217. A Platt map (p = sigmoid(0.7237·logit − 1.5665)) fitted on the validation split brings it to 0.032, and the Brier score from 0.168 to 0.099. The map is monotonic, so AUROC is identical before and after — 0.8833 on the internal test split either way, which is the check that nothing was traded away.

It also moved the decision threshold, which matters more than the probabilities for anyone thresholding them. 0.5 was a convention and was never right for this head: on the raw scale its own optimum is 0.73. On the calibrated scale the threshold chosen on validation is 0.34, and it scores MCC 0.5213 on test against 0.4934 for the old raw-0.5 default — close to the 0.5284 upper bound that could only be found by looking at the test labels. Both the map and the threshold are recorded in the head's metadata, and the CLI and the desktop application both read them from there rather than compiling in a number.

Because the head now reports different numbers from the same weights, it is a different model: its version went to 1.1.0 and its build id changed, so a lockfile taken before the calibration correctly fails against it.

The threshold is a property of a distribution, not of the head, and this one does not suit every set. On the CAID3 reference set, MCC falls from 0.7292 to 0.7096, F1 from 0.8182 to 0.7788 and balanced accuracy from 0.8777 to 0.8250 at the new threshold — because 0.34 calibrated is about 0.78 raw, and that set wants a lower cut than ours does. The reason is measurable rather than hand-waved: 31.6% of CAID's assessed residues are disordered against 17.9% of our internal test split's, so it is nearly twice as positive a set, with a PDB-derived definition of disorder rather than DisProt's. AUROC and AUPRC are identical (0.9410 and 0.8996), which is why those are the figures to compare against published work. If you threshold these probabilities for a decision of your own, the right cut depends on your class balance and on what a false positive costs you. Calibration is what makes that reasoning possible; it does not make the choice for you.

What this is calibrated against is the annotation, not nature. DisProt records disorder demonstrated experimentally and unannotated residues are treated as ordered in training. If that under-reports disorder — and it does, by an unknown amount — these probabilities inherit it. A calibrated 0.3 means "three in ten of residues like this are annotated disordered in DisProt", which is a weaker statement than it looks.

Intervals on every figure above are bootstrapped over proteins, not residues. Neighbouring residues almost always share a label, so resampling residues would report an interval several times too narrow.

docs.title: How wrong is a regressor's number likely to be?
docs.text:
Each of the three regressors now reports an interval beside its point, fitted by split conformal prediction on the validation split and measured on the held-out one:

Head 90% interval Coverage achieved Held-out MAE stability ±1.33 kcal/mol 93.7% 0.53 kcal/mol solubility ±38.9 percentage points 91.1% 18.8 pp burial ±0.237 RSA 87.5% 0.115 RSA

Read the stability row before acting on a ddG. A predicted −0.78 kcal/mol comes with an interval of −2.11 to +0.55, which spans zero: at 90% confidence that head cannot tell you whether the mutation is destabilising at all. A prediction of −1.59 gives −2.92 to −0.26, which does not. That distinction is the useful content, and a point estimate alone hides it.

Read the solubility row the same way. ±39 percentage points on a 0–100 scale is most of the range, which is the honest measure of how much a single solubility number is worth. Intervals there can extend past 100%, because the head is an unbounded regressor that was never constrained to the physical range — an interval reaching 139% is the head saying it does not know.

Coverage is measured, not assumed, and burial falls short. A conformal guarantee assumes the calibration and held-out sets are exchangeable. This project's splits are deliberately not: the dataset builder clusters by sequence identity so near-identical proteins cannot straddle a split, which makes the held-out set systematically more distant than a random sample would be. That is the right way to build the splits and it costs the guarantee its exactness. Burial achieves 87.5% where 90% was asked for, 76.0% where 80% was, and 43.3% where 50% was — short at every level.

Coverage is also marginal, not conditional. The half-width is constant, so the interval is wider than needed where the head is reliable and narrower than needed where it is not. For burial at the 90% level, coverage runs from 96.8% for residues predicted to be buried down to 79.1% in the middle of the range. Somebody holding a mid-range prediction has a 79% interval labelled 90%. Each model card lists the conditional coverage by band.

One more caveat specific to stability, and it is worse than an earlier version of this page said. Its 37,983 calibration residuals come from the validation split, which the dataset manifest records as 18 sequence-identity clusters of wild-type proteins; coverage was then measured on a test split of 24. This page previously said 36, a figure nothing supports — the manifest is the source, and it is in datasets/cards/stability/manifest.json. Residuals from one wild-type protein are correlated, so each quantile rests on something nearer 18 independent observations than 37,983, and coverage on a protein unlike those 18 may be worse than the table says.

docs.title: Should I trust every residue equally?
docs.text:
No, and the disorder head now says which ones. How far the calibrated probability sits from the decision threshold orders residues by how likely the call is to be wrong, measured on the held-out split:

Minimum confidence Residues kept Error among them 0.00 (everything) 100% 15.7% 0.05 89% 12.0% 0.10 80% 9.3% 0.20 66% 6.5% 0.25 57% 5.3%

The signal captures 55% of the error reduction an oracle shows is available — an oracle being a rule that discards exactly the wrong calls. Half of what is there. Worth having, not a guarantee.

Every disorder output carries a confidence column. predict --min-confidence <c> additionally marks the rows below a cut-off in a low_confidence column and prints what that cut-off was measured to buy. Nothing is ever removed: a table quietly missing rows looks exactly like a complete one, and the cut-off is the caller's because the right one depends on what a wrong call costs them.

A signal that failed, recorded so nobody re-tests it. The obvious out-of-domain proxy — whether the 5-mer centred on a residue was seen in training — carries no information about error. Its area under the risk–coverage curve was 0.171 against 0.158 for discarding residues at random, so marginally worse than nothing, despite 44.9% of held-out residues sitting on an unseen 5-mer. Error on novel k-mers is not higher than on familiar ones. A plausible story about why a signal should work is not evidence that it does.

docs.title: Can I continue a run that was interrupted?
docs.text:
Yes, and the thing worth checking is not that it continues but that continuing gives the same answer as not having stopped.

--checkpoint <file> records results as they are produced and syncs them to disk after every chunk of --chunk sequences. Running the same command again continues from the last complete chunk. The results file is written only when the run finishes.

Verified byte-identical. On a twelve-sequence file predicted in chunks of four, a checkpoint was cut back to one complete chunk plus a half-written record — what a process killed mid-write leaves behind — and the run was started again. It reported the incomplete tail, dropped it, continued from chunk one, and produced the same 854 rows as the uninterrupted run, byte for byte, with the same output digest recorded in both manifests. The checkpoint files themselves also ended up identical.

This holds because the chunk boundaries are fixed and recorded rather than falling wherever the interruption did. Sequences are batched for embedding within their chunk, and batch composition changes the order of floating-point sums, so an arbitrary cut would not reproduce. The cost is that the chunk size is itself a setting that changes the numbers:

any --chunk, with --batch-tokens 0 identical to a run with no checkpoint --chunk 1 or 4, at the CPU default of 8192 1 of 853 burial values differs, by 0.0001

That is the same mechanism and the same order of magnitude as the batch-size effect already measured above, and it is why the chunk size is recorded in every run manifest and compared by opendna merge.

Resuming is refused, naming the field that differs, when the input bytes, the chunk size, the head build, the head's weights digest, the embedding model, the device, the batch size, the mutation file or the confidence cut-off is not what the checkpoint was written with. A file that is not a checkpoint is refused without being modified.

docs.title: Can I run it without a network?
docs.text:
opendna stage --to /mnt/usb/opendna-models   # on a connected machine
opendna --models ./opendna-models --offline selftest

stage writes one directory holding the four heads, their model cards, the embedding model's own files, models.lock, a sha256sums.txt in the format sha256sum -c reads, and a LICENSES.md. It copies what the staging machine already resolved rather than re-fetching on the target, so the bundle is what was tested. It refuses to stage an installation that does not verify.

--offline is a hard promise: nothing reaches the network, and a missing embedding model is an error naming the two files it wanted and the command that makes them, rather than a stall.

Checked: with HF_HOME pointed at an empty directory so the cache held nothing, --offline passed all seventeen self-test checks against a staged bundle and produced disorder values identical to the online run. sha256sum -c sha256sums.txt verified all fourteen files (four heads with weights, metadata and card each, plus the embedding model's two). With nothing staged, --offline exits 3 with the staging instructions.

docs.title: What does a failure tell my pipeline?
docs.text:
0 it worked — 1 an unanticipated failure report it 2 the command asked for something that does not exist fix the command 3 the installation is wrong fix the machine; retrying will not help 4 the data is wrong fix the input; retrying will not help 5 the checks ran and did not hold do not use results from this machine

Anything not classified is 1, deliberately: a failure nobody anticipated is not one a caller can be told how to handle.

predict streams results to standard output, so a failing run leaves standard output empty — a pipe collecting results never receives an error as though it were data.

Checked: all twelve cases in tests/exit_codes.rs, against the compiled binary, with the corrupt and swapped fixtures built from a copy of the real models.

docs.title: Can I show what produced a result?
docs.text:
Every run that writes an output file writes out.manifest.json beside it: input path and SHA-256 of the bytes read, output path and SHA-256, row count, head task/version/build/weights-hash, embedding model, device, batch size, UTC start, wall-clock duration, the arguments as given, the head's licence, and the model card's limitations.

The input is hashed from the bytes in memory rather than by re-reading the file, so the digest describes what was used even when the input arrived through a pipe and has no path.

The embedding model is not hashed by default: at 568 MB it costs about as long as a small run. A staged bundle already records the digest, so a staged install carries it for free; otherwise the field is null and sha256_source says why. An absent field with a reason is honest. A missing field somebody assumes was checked is not.

docs.title: What are my obligations if I pass this on?
docs.text:
Three heads are Apache-2.0. The solubility head is CC BY-SA 2.1 JP: it is trained on eSOL, which carries that licence, and because the licence is share-alike — and because whether trained weights are a derivative work of their training data is an open legal question this project will not answer in its own favour — the weights carry the same terms.

A staged bundle is a redistribution. opendna stage writes a LICENSES.md grouping heads by licence and stating when passing the bundle on carries obligations, and each card travels beside its weights with the attribution its licence requires. Required attribution for eSOL: "eSOL © Hideki Taguchi (Tokyo Institute of Technology) licensed under CC Attribution-Share Alike 2.1 Japan".

All of it is read out of the model cards rather than written into the program, so a notice cannot claim terms the file beside the weights does not. A head whose card declares no licence is reported as unstated and treated as possibly obliging.

docs.title: Can several runs go at once on one machine?
docs.text:
Only against a staged bundle. Measured:

Two runs loading the embedding model through the Hugging Face cache one failed, exit 3 Three runs against a directory produced by opendna stage all three fine

The cache is not safe for two processes to read at the same time; on Windows the second is refused the weights file by the operating system. A staged bundle is opened read-only and shares without trouble. So a node running several parts of a split in parallel needs opendna stage once and then --models <bundle> --offline on each task, which is what the cluster section of the CLI README now says. The error a failed concurrent run prints names this as the likely cause.

docs.title: What has not been checked
docs.text:
Stated plainly, because a validation document that lists only successes is marketing.

  • One machine. Every number here comes from a single Windows workstation with an RTX 2000 Ada. CI builds on three operating systems, but the measurements above were not repeated on them. Cross-platform numerical agreement is untested.
  • No GPU other than one. The finding that batching costs time on a GPU is from that one card. Another may behave differently, which is why --batch-tokens is a flag.
  • Timing figures are approximate. The CPU gain from batching measured a tenth in one session and a sixth in another. Two earlier attempts, taken while a compile competed for the cores, produced an overstated figure and then none at all. If you benchmark, interleave the settings and report the spread.
  • Tolerances in the self-test are a judgement, set on one machine, not a measured bound on acceptable variation.
  • No clinical or diagnostic validation of any kind. These are research tools. The stability head in particular is a ranking signal at ~0.44 Spearman out of domain.
  • Metrics on each head's own test split are not comparable to published leaderboard figures without running that leaderboard's protocol. The disorder head's CAID3 number was produced by running the CAID protocol; the others' were not.
  • No signed installers. Binaries are unsigned, so operating systems will warn. Code-signing certificates have not been obtained.
  • The regressors' intervals rest on an assumption the splits break. See the section above. Conformal coverage assumes calibration and held-out sets are exchangeable; clustering by sequence identity makes them deliberately not. The achieved coverage is measured rather than assumed, and for burial it falls short at every level.
  • Resuming was checked on small runs, on the CPU only. The byte-identical result above comes from files of two to twelve sequences predicted in two to twelve chunks, with a real process kill in one case and a hand-truncated checkpoint in the others. All four heads were covered. What was not exercised is the thing the feature is for: a run of tens of thousands of sequences interrupted hours in. Nor was any of it repeated on the GPU, where the batch default differs.
  • Nothing detects out-of-domain input. The disorder head reports a confidence that predicts error (see above), but that is not the same thing: a sequence from a family it never saw can still produce a confident wrong answer. The one out-of-domain proxy measured here, whether a residue's 5-mer was seen in training, carried no information about error at all.

docs.title: Reproducing the checks
docs.text:
opendna models --check models.lock   # the install is what it was
opendna selftest                     # it computes what it recorded
opendna --device cpu selftest        # and on the CPU too, where a GPU exists
cargo test --workspace               # unit and contract tests
cargo test --release -p opendna-cli -- --ignored   # the two needing inference

The exit-code test needs trained heads installed and skips with a message when they are absent, because a test that fails on every machine without them gets disabled and then checks nothing at all.
